--- title: "Session 13 — Big Data Analytics Fundamentals" subtitle: "The five Vs · Four types of analytics · When one machine stops being enough · HDFS · The toolkit" --- ::: {.callout-note} **This chapter is about what changes when the data no longer fits on your laptop.** **Assumed knowledge:** Sessions 2–3 — pandas, loading and cleaning. Nothing else. **The one idea to take away:** "big data" is not a size, it is a **symptom**. It begins at the point where one machine stops being enough — and that point arrives far later than most people think. Every demo in this chapter runs on your laptop. ::: ## 🎯 Learning outcomes {#sec-s13-outcomes} By the end of this chapter you can: 1. Explain the five Vs and say which one actually causes trouble in a given project. 2. Measure the point at which pandas starts to struggle on your own machine. 3. Process a file larger than memory using chunks. 4. Name the four types of analytics and give an example of each. 5. Explain how HDFS stores a file across many machines and survives a failure. 6. Place the main big-data tools on a map and say what each is for. 7. Say when **not** to use big-data tools. ## How this chapter is organised {#sec-s13-organisation} | Part | Question it answers | |---|---| | [A — What makes data big](#sec-s13-a) | *When does normal stop working?* | | [B — Four types of analytics](#sec-s13-b) | *What questions can you ask of it?* | | [C — Distributed storage](#sec-s13-c) | *How do you keep a file too big for one disk?* | | [D — The toolkit](#sec-s13-d) | *What are all these names, and which do I need?* | # Part A — What makes data big {#sec-s13-a} ## 1. The five Vs {#sec-s13-topic-1} **Big data is usually described with five words beginning with V.** They are useful as a checklist, provided you remember that **only one of them is usually your actual problem.** | V | Means | The problem it creates | |---|---|---| | **Volume** | how much there is | it does not fit in memory or on one disk | | **Velocity** | how fast it arrives | you cannot store it before the next batch arrives | | **Variety** | how many shapes it comes in | text, images, JSON and tables need different handling | | **Veracity** | how much you can trust it | sensors fail, users lie, systems disagree | | **Value** | whether it is worth anything | most of it is never used | ::: {.callout-tip title="🧠 Analogy — the library"} **Volume** — the library has ten million books, and no room for shelves. **Velocity** — twelve thousand new books arrive every hour. **Variety** — some are books, some are scrolls, some are audio recordings. **Veracity** — some are unreliable, and some are simply wrong. **Value** — nine million of them will never be opened. **A library with a volume problem needs a bigger building. One with a velocity problem needs a faster door.** They are different problems with different solutions, and calling both "big data" hides that. ::: ## 2. Where one machine stops being enough {#sec-s13-topic-2} **The honest threshold is not a number of rows. It is the point where the work no longer fits in memory.** A rough guide: pandas comfortably handles data up to about **one fifth of your RAM**, because operations make copies. Beyond that your machine starts swapping to disk and everything slows by orders of magnitude. ### Demo 1 — measure it on your own machine ::: {#1343670a .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np, pandas as pd, time def timed(f): t = time.perf_counter(); out = f(); return out, time.perf_counter() - t rng = np.random.default_rng(71) print(f"{'rows':>12} {'memory':>12} {'groupby time':>14} {'per M rows':>12}") print("-" * 54) for n in [10_000, 100_000, 1_000_000, 4_000_000]: df = pd.DataFrame({ "shop": rng.integers(0, 50, n), "amount": rng.normal(500, 120, n), }) mem = df.memory_usage(deep=True).sum() / 1e6 _, secs = timed(lambda: df.groupby("shop")["amount"].mean()) print(f"{n:>12,} {mem:>10.1f} MB {secs*1000:>12.1f} ms {secs/(n/1e6)*1000:>10.1f} ms") print("\nThe cost per million rows stays roughly flat — pandas is not struggling yet.") print("It struggles when the data plus its working copies stop fitting in RAM.") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` rows memory groupby time per M rows ------------------------------------------------------ 10,000 0.2 MB 2.5 ms 254.1 ms 100,000 1.6 MB 1.5 ms 15.2 ms 1,000,000 16.0 MB 14.1 ms 14.1 ms 4,000,000 64.0 MB 38.8 ms 9.7 ms The cost per million rows stays roughly flat — pandas is not struggling yet. It struggles when the data plus its working copies stop fitting in RAM. ``` ::: ::: ### Demo 2 — how much memory a realistic table needs ::: {#c672ecb7 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np, pandas as pd rng = np.random.default_rng(72) n = 200_000 df = pd.DataFrame({ "id": np.arange(n), "city": rng.choice(["Mumbai", "Delhi", "Pune", "Chennai"], n), "amount": rng.normal(500, 120, n), "ts": pd.date_range("2024-01-01", periods=n, freq="min"), }) per_row = df.memory_usage(deep=True).sum() / n print(f"this table: {df.memory_usage(deep=True).sum()/1e6:.1f} MB for {n:,} rows " f"({per_row:.0f} bytes per row)\n") print(f"{'rows':>16} {'estimated size':>16} {'fits in 16 GB RAM?'}") for rows in [1e6, 1e7, 1e8, 1e9]: gb = rows * per_row / 1e9 verdict = "yes, comfortably" if gb < 3 else "tight — use chunks" if gb < 16 else "NO — needs a cluster" print(f"{rows:>16,.0f} {gb:>13.1f} GB {verdict}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` this table: 17.3 MB for 200,000 rows (87 bytes per row) rows estimated size fits in 16 GB RAM? 1,000,000 0.1 GB yes, comfortably 10,000,000 0.9 GB yes, comfortably 100,000,000 8.7 GB tight — use chunks 1,000,000,000 86.5 GB NO — needs a cluster ``` ::: ::: ### Demo 3 — two ways to survive a file bigger than memory **Before reaching for a cluster, two techniques solve most "too big" problems on one machine.** ::: {#60ffe64e .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np, pandas as pd, tempfile, os folder = tempfile.mkdtemp() path = os.path.join(folder, "transactions.csv") rng = np.random.default_rng(73) n = 300_000 pd.DataFrame({ "shop": rng.integers(0, 50, n), "city": rng.choice(["Mumbai", "Delhi", "Pune"], n), "amount": rng.normal(500, 120, n).round(2), }).to_csv(path, index=False) print(f"file on disk: {os.path.getsize(path)/1e6:.1f} MB, {n:,} rows\n") # --- TECHNIQUE 1: chunking. Never hold the whole file at once. ------------- running_total, running_count = 0.0, 0 per_city = {} for chunk in pd.read_csv(path, chunksize=50_000): # 50,000 rows at a time running_total += chunk["amount"].sum() running_count += len(chunk) for city, total in chunk.groupby("city")["amount"].sum().items(): per_city[city] = per_city.get(city, 0) + total print(f"CHUNKED: mean amount {running_total/running_count:.2f} over {running_count:,} rows") print(f" totals per city: { {k: round(v) for k, v in per_city.items()} }") print(f" peak memory held: one chunk of 50,000 rows, not {n:,}") # --- TECHNIQUE 2: read only what you need --------------------------------- narrow = pd.read_csv(path, usecols=["city", "amount"]) wide = pd.read_csv(path) print(f"\nCOLUMN SELECTION: all columns {wide.memory_usage(deep=True).sum()/1e6:.1f} MB") print(f" two columns {narrow.memory_usage(deep=True).sum()/1e6:.1f} MB") # --- BONUS: the right dtype often halves the memory ----------------------- compact = wide.copy() compact["city"] = compact["city"].astype("category") compact["shop"] = compact["shop"].astype("int8") print(f"\nDTYPES: before {wide.memory_usage(deep=True).sum()/1e6:.1f} MB" f" → after {compact.memory_usage(deep=True).sum()/1e6:.1f} MB") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` file on disk: 4.7 MB, 300,000 rows CHUNKED: mean amount 499.77 over 300,000 rows totals per city: {'Delhi': 49904568, 'Mumbai': 50027779, 'Pune': 49998660} peak memory held: one chunk of 50,000 rows, not 300,000 COLUMN SELECTION: all columns 23.4 MB two columns 21.0 MB DTYPES: before 23.4 MB → after 3.0 MB ``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-warning title="⚠️ Try these before you build a cluster"} Chunking, selecting columns and fixing dtypes routinely turn a "we need Spark" problem back into a laptop problem. **A distributed cluster costs money, expertise and debugging time.** Spend a day on the three techniques above first — most of the time, that is the whole solution. ::: # Part B — Four types of analytics {#sec-s13-b} ## 3. The four questions {#sec-s13-topic-3} **Every analysis is one of four kinds, in increasing order of difficulty and value.** | Type | Question | Example | Covered in | |---|---|---|---| | **Descriptive** | *What happened?* | sales fell 12% last quarter | Sessions 7–8 | | **Diagnostic** | *Why did it happen?* | the fall was entirely in one region | Session 8 | | **Predictive** | *What will happen?* | next quarter will fall another 5% | Sessions 9–11 | | **Prescriptive** | *What should we do?* | move stock to the region that is growing | Session 16 | ```{mermaid} flowchart LR D["Descriptive
what happened?"] --> G["Diagnostic
why?"] G --> P["Predictive
what next?"] P --> X["Prescriptive
what should we do?"] ``` ### Demo 4 — all four on one dataset ::: {#31b3e5c5 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np, pandas as pd rng = np.random.default_rng(74) months = pd.date_range("2024-01-01", periods=12, freq="MS") regions = ["North", "South", "West"] rows = [] for i, m in enumerate(months): for r in regions: trend = {"North": -900, "South": 400, "West": 500}[r] * i base = {"North": 50_000, "South": 40_000, "West": 30_000}[r] rows.append({"month": m, "region": r, "sales": base + trend + rng.normal(0, 800)}) sales = pd.DataFrame(rows) # 1. DESCRIPTIVE — what happened? by_month = sales.groupby("month")["sales"].sum() change = (by_month.iloc[-1] - by_month.iloc[0]) / by_month.iloc[0] print(f"DESCRIPTIVE : total sales moved {change:+.1%} across the year") # 2. DIAGNOSTIC — why? by_region = sales.groupby("region").apply( lambda g: (g.sort_values("month")["sales"].iloc[-1] - g.sort_values("month")["sales"].iloc[0]), include_groups=False) print("DIAGNOSTIC : change by region over the year") for r, v in by_region.items(): print(f" {r:<6} {v:>+10,.0f}") print(f" → the decline is entirely {by_region.idxmin()}; the others grew") # 3. PREDICTIVE — what next? from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression x = np.arange(len(by_month)).reshape(-1, 1) trend_model = LinearRegression().fit(x, by_month.values) next3 = trend_model.predict([[12], [13], [14]]) print(f"PREDICTIVE : next three months ≈ {', '.join(f'{v:,.0f}' for v in next3)}") # 4. PRESCRIPTIVE — what should we do? growing = by_region[by_region > 0].index.tolist() print(f"PRESCRIPTIVE: shift investment from {by_region.idxmin()} to {', '.join(growing)};") print(f" re-examine {by_region.idxmin()} before writing it off") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` DESCRIPTIVE : total sales moved -0.6% across the year DIAGNOSTIC : change by region over the year North -9,451 South +4,045 West +4,639 → the decline is entirely North; the others grew PREDICTIVE : next three months ≈ 120,147, 120,128, 120,110 PRESCRIPTIVE: shift investment from North to South, West; re-examine North before writing it off ``` ::: ::: **Notice the increasing difficulty.** Descriptive is a `groupby`. Prescriptive needs a prediction *and* a judgement about what to do with it — which is why the last one is never fully automatic. # Part C — Distributed storage {#sec-s13-c} ## 4. How HDFS works {#sec-s13-topic-4} **HDFS — the Hadoop Distributed File System — stores one enormous file across many ordinary machines, and keeps working when some of them fail.** Three ideas do all the work: | Idea | What it means | |---|---| | **Blocks** | the file is cut into fixed-size pieces, typically 128 MB | | **Replication** | every block is stored on **three** different machines | | **Write once** | files are appended to, never edited in the middle | ```{mermaid} flowchart TB F["one 400 MB file"] --> B1["block 1
128 MB"] F --> B2["block 2
128 MB"] F --> B3["block 3
128 MB"] F --> B4["block 4
16 MB"] B1 --> N["NameNode
remembers which block
is on which machine"] B2 --> N B3 --> N B4 --> N N --> D1["DataNode 1"] N --> D2["DataNode 2"] N --> D3["DataNode 3"] ``` The **NameNode** holds the index — which blocks make up which file, and where each copy lives. The **DataNodes** hold the actual blocks. **The NameNode never touches the data itself**, which is why one modest machine can index petabytes. ### Demo 5 — block splitting and replication, simulated ::: {#0baf5fe3 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} import math def plan_storage(file_gb, block_mb=128, replication=3, datanodes=6): blocks = math.ceil(file_gb * 1024 / block_mb) copies = blocks * replication print(f"file size : {file_gb} GB") print(f"block size : {block_mb} MB") print(f"blocks : {blocks:,}") print(f"copies stored : {blocks:,} × {replication} = {copies:,}") print(f"disk used : {file_gb * replication} GB " f"({replication}× the file, the price of surviving failures)") print(f"blocks per node : about {copies // datanodes:,} across {datanodes} machines") print(f"machines that can fail without data loss: {replication - 1}") plan_storage(400) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` file size : 400 GB block size : 128 MB blocks : 3,200 copies stored : 3,200 × 3 = 9,600 disk used : 1200 GB (3× the file, the price of surviving failures) blocks per node : about 1,600 across 6 machines machines that can fail without data loss: 2 ``` ::: ::: ### Demo 6 — why replication is worth 3× the disk ::: {#8a3dcbfb .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np rng = np.random.default_rng(75) n_nodes, annual_failure_rate, trials = 200, 0.04, 20_000 for replication in [1, 2, 3]: lost = 0 for _ in range(trials): failed = rng.random(n_nodes) < annual_failure_rate # a block is lost only if every machine holding a copy fails holders = rng.choice(n_nodes, replication, replace=False) if failed[holders].all(): lost += 1 print(f"replication {replication}: chance a given block is lost in a year " f"= {lost/trials:.4%}") print(f"\n(with {n_nodes} machines and a {annual_failure_rate:.0%} annual failure rate)") print("Three copies turns near-certain annual data loss into a negligible risk.") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` replication 1: chance a given block is lost in a year = 4.2350% replication 2: chance a given block is lost in a year = 0.1050% replication 3: chance a given block is lost in a year = 0.0100% (with 200 machines and a 4% annual failure rate) Three copies turns near-certain annual data loss into a negligible risk. ``` ::: ::: ## 5. Talking to HDFS {#sec-s13-topic-5} **HDFS commands look deliberately like ordinary shell commands.** These need a running Hadoop cluster, so they are shown rather than executed here. ```bash # List a directory in the cluster hdfs dfs -ls /user/data/logs # Found 1 items # -rw-r--r-- 3 hadoop supergroup 1099511627776 2024-01-01 12:00 /user/data/logs/clicks.csv # ↑ # this 3 is the replication factor: every block exists on three machines # Copy a local file INTO the cluster hdfs dfs -put ./local_logs.csv /user/data/logs/ # Copy a file back OUT of the cluster hdfs dfs -get /user/data/logs/clicks.csv ./downloaded.csv # Peek at the first lines of a 1 TB file, without downloading it hdfs dfs -cat /user/data/logs/clicks.csv | head -20 # How is this file actually laid out across the cluster? hdfs fsck /user/data/logs/clicks.csv -files -blocks -locations ``` ::: {.callout-important title="🔓 Running this yourself"} You do not need a cluster to complete this course. Three options, easiest first: | Option | What you get | Effort | |---|---|---| | **PySpark local mode** | everything in Session 14 except the `hdfs dfs` commands | `pip install pyspark`, needs Java 17 | | **Docker** | a real single-node Hadoop, so `hdfs dfs` commands work | one `docker run` | | **A hosted sandbox** | a full cluster in a browser | sign-up only | **Every executable cell in this chapter and the next runs in local mode.** The `bash` blocks above are reference — they are the commands you would type against a real cluster. ::: ::: {.callout-warning title="⚠️ HDFS is terrible at small files"} One 128 MB file uses one block and one entry in the NameNode's index. **A million 128-byte files use a million entries** — and the NameNode keeps its index in memory. Small files exhaust the cluster's index long before they exhaust its disks. **The fix is always the same: combine small files into large ones before storing them.** ::: ::: {#e5a22b29 .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} def namenode_pressure(total_gb, avg_file_mb): files = total_gb * 1024 / avg_file_mb # roughly 150 bytes of NameNode memory per file plus per block mem_gb = files * 150 * 2 / 1e9 print(f"{total_gb:>6} GB as {avg_file_mb:>6.2f} MB files → {files:>12,.0f} files, " f"NameNode index ≈ {mem_gb:>7.2f} GB") print("Same amount of data, different file sizes:") for size in [256, 64, 1, 0.1]: namenode_pressure(10_000, size) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Same amount of data, different file sizes: 10000 GB as 256.00 MB files → 40,000 files, NameNode index ≈ 0.01 GB 10000 GB as 64.00 MB files → 160,000 files, NameNode index ≈ 0.05 GB 10000 GB as 1.00 MB files → 10,240,000 files, NameNode index ≈ 3.07 GB 10000 GB as 0.10 MB files → 102,400,000 files, NameNode index ≈ 30.72 GB ``` ::: ::: # Part D — The toolkit {#sec-s13-d} ## 6. What all the names are {#sec-s13-topic-6} **The big-data ecosystem is a pile of names. Sorted by what they do, it is short.** ```{mermaid} flowchart TB subgraph ING["Getting data in"] K["Kafka
streams of events"] S["Sqoop / Flume
bulk import"] end subgraph ST["Storing it"] H["HDFS
files across machines"] HB["HBase / Cassandra
fast lookups"] end subgraph PR["Processing it"] MR["MapReduce
the original, disk-based"] SP["Spark
the successor, in memory"] end subgraph QU["Querying it"] HV["Hive
SQL over big files"] SS["Spark SQL"] end ING --> ST --> PR --> QU ``` | Tool | One sentence | Session | |---|---|---| | **HDFS** | stores files across many machines | this one | | **YARN** | decides which machine runs which job | this one | | **MapReduce** | the original processing model — simple, and slow | 14 | | **Spark** | the successor — same idea, kept in memory, far faster | 14 | | **Hive** | lets you write SQL against files in HDFS | 14 | | **Kafka** | carries continuous streams of events | mentioned only | | **HBase / Cassandra** | databases for fast lookups at scale | 15 | | **MongoDB** | a document database for flexible records | 15 | ## 7. When not to use any of this {#sec-s13-topic-7} **Distributed tools have a fixed overhead. Below a certain size they are slower than pandas, not faster.** ### Demo 7 — the overhead, quantified ::: {#34bc2c59 .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np, pandas as pd, time rng = np.random.default_rng(76) CLUSTER_STARTUP_S = 8.0 # a real Spark session takes seconds to start PER_TASK_OVERHEAD = 0.15 # scheduling, serialising, shuffling print(f"{'rows':>12} {'pandas':>10} {'distributed (modelled)':>24} winner") print("-" * 62) for n in [10_000, 100_000, 1_000_000, 5_000_000]: df = pd.DataFrame({"k": rng.integers(0, 100, n), "v": rng.normal(size=n)}) t = time.perf_counter() df.groupby("k")["v"].mean() pandas_s = time.perf_counter() - t # A cluster splits the work but pays startup and coordination costs. partitions = max(4, n // 250_000) dist_s = CLUSTER_STARTUP_S + PER_TASK_OVERHEAD * partitions + (pandas_s / 8) winner = "pandas" if pandas_s < dist_s else "distributed" print(f"{n:>12,} {pandas_s*1000:>8.1f} ms {dist_s*1000:>21,.0f} ms {winner}") print("\nThe modelled cluster never wins here, because none of these datasets is") print("large enough to repay an 8-second startup. That crossover is the number") print("you must find for yourself — Session 14 measures it with real Spark.") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` rows pandas distributed (modelled) winner -------------------------------------------------------------- 10,000 0.5 ms 8,600 ms pandas 100,000 0.9 ms 8,600 ms pandas 1,000,000 10.9 ms 8,601 ms pandas 5,000,000 53.3 ms 11,007 ms pandas The modelled cluster never wins here, because none of these datasets is large enough to repay an 8-second startup. That crossover is the number you must find for yourself — Session 14 measures it with real Spark. ``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-warning title="⚠️ 'Big data' is a claim that needs evidence"} Before adopting distributed tooling, answer three questions with numbers: 1. **How large is the data actually?** — in GB, measured, not estimated 2. **Have I tried chunking, column selection and dtypes?** — Demo 3 3. **How long does the job take now, and how long is acceptable?** If the answer to 3 is "four minutes, and ten would be fine", **you do not have a big-data problem.** You have a four-minute job. ::: ### ❓ Check yourself **Q1.** A hospital receives 50,000 sensor readings per second and must react within a second. Which V is the problem? - (a) Volume. - (b) **Velocity.** - (c) Value. **Q2.** A 40 GB CSV must be summarised on a laptop with 16 GB of RAM. What do you try first? - (a) Buy a cluster. - (b) **Read it in chunks and select only the needed columns.** - (c) Sample 1% and hope. **Q3.** "Sales fell because the North region lost its two largest customers." Which type? - (a) Descriptive. - (b) **Diagnostic.** - (c) Prescriptive. **Q4.** HDFS replicates every block three times. What does that cost and buy? - (a) Costs nothing, buys speed. - (b) **Costs 3× the disk, buys survival when up to two machines holding a block fail.** - (c) Costs 3× the time, buys accuracy. **Q5.** Your cluster has plenty of disk free but the NameNode is out of memory. Likely cause? - (a) A single enormous file. - (b) **Millions of tiny files, each needing an index entry.** - (c) Replication set too low. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answers"} **A1 — (b).** The total volume may be modest; the difficulty is the rate and the deadline. **A2 — (b).** Demo 3. Chunking plus column selection solves most of these. **A3 — (b).** It explains *why*, which is the diagnostic question. **A4 — (b).** Demo 6 measured the failure probabilities. **A5 — (b).** The small-files problem — the NameNode's index lives in memory. ::: # 🎯 Tasks {#sec-s13-tasks} ::: {.callout-note title="✏️ Practise"} **Task 1 — Find your own limit.** Extend Demo 1 to 10 and 20 million rows. **Report the row count at which the time per million rows starts to rise**, and how much RAM your machine has. **Task 2 — Chunk a real job.** Using the chunking pattern from Demo 3, compute the **median** amount per city. **Explain why this is harder than the mean** and what you did about it. **Task 3 — Classify the questions.** Which of the four types: "which products are most often returned?"; "will this customer return this item?"; "why did returns rise in March?"; "which items should we stop stocking?" **Task 4 — Size a cluster.** You have 8 TB of logs, a 128 MB block size and replication 3. **Report the number of blocks, the total disk needed, and how many 4 TB machines you would buy.** ::: :::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solutions"} ::: {#398cefeb .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} import math, numpy as np, pandas as pd print("Task 2 — the mean can be computed from running totals, so chunks combine") print(" trivially. The median cannot: you need all the values for a city at once,") print(" or an approximation. Two workable approaches:") print(" a) collect just the one column per city across chunks, then take the median") print(" b) use an approximate quantile from a histogram built chunk by chunk") print("\nTask 3") for q, kind in [("which products are most often returned?", "DESCRIPTIVE"), ("will this customer return this item?", "PREDICTIVE"), ("why did returns rise in March?", "DIAGNOSTIC"), ("which items should we stop stocking?", "PRESCRIPTIVE")]: print(f" {q:<44} {kind}") # Task 4 tb, block_mb, rep, disk_per_node_tb = 8, 128, 3, 4 blocks = math.ceil(tb * 1024 * 1024 / block_mb) total_tb = tb * rep print(f"\nTask 4 — {blocks:,} blocks; {total_tb} TB of disk needed;") print(f" {math.ceil(total_tb / disk_per_node_tb)} machines at {disk_per_node_tb} TB each,") print(f" and in practice more, since you never fill a cluster to 100%.") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Task 2 — the mean can be computed from running totals, so chunks combine trivially. The median cannot: you need all the values for a city at once, or an approximation. Two workable approaches: a) collect just the one column per city across chunks, then take the median b) use an approximate quantile from a histogram built chunk by chunk Task 3 which products are most often returned? DESCRIPTIVE will this customer return this item? PREDICTIVE why did returns rise in March? DIAGNOSTIC which items should we stop stocking? PRESCRIPTIVE Task 4 — 65,536 blocks; 24 TB of disk needed; 6 machines at 4 TB each, and in practice more, since you never fill a cluster to 100%. ``` ::: ::: :::: ::: {.callout-tip title="✅ Before you move on"} - [ ] I can name the five Vs and say which one a given project actually suffers from - [ ] I have measured where pandas starts to struggle on my own machine - [ ] I can process a file larger than memory using chunks - [ ] I can explain blocks, replication and the NameNode - [ ] I know why HDFS hates small files - [ ] **Easiest thing to forget:** try chunking, column selection and dtypes before reaching for a cluster. They usually turn the problem back into a laptop problem. :::
